session.question: How the sustainability assessment and evaluation frameworks in the district heating and PT evaluation studies are linked, and which method was most used, plus how do they relate to CO2 emissions reduction in the urban transport example?
session.answer:
The district heating (DH) study and the PT (public transport) evaluation studies are linked only at a methodological level: both use sustainability assessment frameworks based on multi-criteria decision analysis (MCDA) to compare alternatives against multiple economic, environmental, and social criteria. In the DH paper, the comparison is explicitly among WSM, TOPSIS, PROMETHEE, ELECTRE, and DEA, with sensitivity analysis of criterion weights and a comparison of AHP-derived versus equal weights. In the PT study, a hybrid MCDA framework combines fuzzy best-worst method (FBWM) for criterion weighting and MABAC for ranking alternatives, with criteria drawn from literature and experts. (daugavietis2022acomparisonof chunk 1, keshavarzghorabaee2021sustainablepublictransportation chunk 1)

The most used method in the DH sustainability literature cited in the excerpt is not stated as a single dominant method beyond the set WSM, TOPSIS, PROMETHEE, ELECTRE, and DEA; however, the excerpt indicates these are the methods frequently applied in district heating sustainability studies. (daugavietis2022acomparisonof chunk 1)

By contrast, the urban transport carbon-emissions example is not an MCDA ranking study but an LCA/GWP-based scenario analysis. It links sustainability assessment to CO2 emissions reduction by quantifying passenger-transport greenhouse-gas impacts across eight mobility scenarios, showing reductions up to 64.28% when trips and travel distances are reduced. Thus, it complements the MCDA-based DH and PT studies by evaluating sustainability directly through life-cycle carbon mitigation rather than through weighted multi-criteria ranking. (montoyatorres2023towardssustainablepassenger chunk 1)

pqac-178e504c: The excerpt describes a study on assessing measures to increase sustainability of an urban transport system. It notes that the authors evaluated managerial measures such as promoting sustainable transport, improving public transport routes, renewing fleets, and switching to cleaner fuels. Their assessment framework considered economic viability as well as social, environmental, and overall sustainability impacts. For the case study in Naberezhnye Chelny, they modeled route-network changes and fleet choices by passenger flow, then evaluated the sustainability of the proposed network using a “radar map” method, which highlights strengths and weaknesses across indicators. The study also included risk analysis in urban bus transportation.
From Irina Makarova, Ksenia Shubenkova, and Anton Pashkevich. Efficiency assessment of measures to increase sustainability of the transport system. Transport, 2021. URL: https://doi.org/10.3846/transport.2021.14996, doi:10.3846/transport.2021.14996.

pqac-a8ec50e4: The excerpt is a 2023 study on sustainable passenger transport in a medium-sized Colombian city. It uses Life-Cycle Assessment (LCA) and Global Warming Potential (GWP) to evaluate eight scenarios for reducing passenger-transport CO2 emissions. The study compares environmental efficiency of measures such as reducing trips and travel distances, increasing public bus fleet size, raising bus occupancy, improving private-vehicle occupancy, expanding electric vehicles, and promoting bicycles. Current annual emissions were 263.98 kt CO2-eq, with reductions up to 64.28% under a 50% reduction in trips per day and distances. This is relevant to evaluation frameworks linking sustainability assessment with emissions reduction.
From Jacid Montoya-Torres, Ortzi Akizu‐Gardoki, Carlos Alejandre, and Maider Iturrondobeitia. Towards sustainable passenger transport: carbon emission reduction scenarios for a medium-sized city. Journal of Cleaner Production, 2023. URL: https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jclepro.2023.138149, doi:10.1016/j.jclepro.2023.138149.

pqac-71b2900f: The excerpt describes a 2023 study on sustainable passenger transport that uses Life-Cycle Assessment (LCA) and Global Warming Potential (GWP) to evaluate carbon emission reduction scenarios in a Colombian medium-sized city. It compares eight mobility policies, including reducing trips and distances, increasing public bus fleet and occupancy, increasing private vehicle occupancy, adding electric vehicles, and promoting bicycles. The current passenger transport emissions are 263.98 kt CO2-eq, with reductions ranging from 5.06% to 64.28% depending on the scenario. The study concludes that managing mobility and restricting commuting can be the most sustainable measure for life-cycle carbon emission reduction.
From Jacid Montoya-Torres, Ortzi Akizu‐Gardoki, Carlos Alejandre, and Maider Iturrondobeitia. Towards sustainable passenger transport: carbon emission reduction scenarios for a medium-sized city. Journal of Cleaner Production, 2023. URL: https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jclepro.2023.138149, doi:10.1016/j.jclepro.2023.138149.

pqac-db62ea04: The excerpt describes a study that evaluates sustainable public transportation in Tehran using a hybrid multi-criteria decision-making framework that combines fuzzy best-worst method (FBWM) for weighting criteria and MABAC for ranking alternatives. It identifies sustainability assessment as a challenge for policy makers and notes that criteria were drawn from literature and expert opinion. The framework found metro and e-hailing to be the most sustainable options, with economic/financial sustainability, service availability, and environmental sustainability as the most important criteria. The study suggests such evaluation frameworks can guide planners in identifying sustainable options and incentive policies.
From Mehdi Keshavarz-Ghorabaee, Maghsoud Amiri, Mohammad Hashemi-Tabatabaei, and Mohammad Ghahremanloo. Sustainable public transportation evaluation using a novel hybrid method based on fuzzy bwm and mabac. The Open Transportation Journal, 2021. contexts.context: The excerpt describes a 2023 study on sustainable passenger transport that uses Life-Cycle Assessment (LCA) and Global Warming Potential (GWP) to evaluate carbon emission reduction scenarios in a Colombian medium-sized city. It compares eight mobility policies, including reducing trips and distances, increasing public bus fleet and occupancy, increasing private vehicle occupancy, adding electric vehicles, and promoting bicycles. The current passenger transport emissions are 263.98 kt CO2-eq, with reductions ranging from 5.06% to 64.28% depending on the scenario. The study concludes that managing mobility and restricting commuting can be the most sustainable measure for life-cycle carbon emission reduction.

session.formatted_answer:
Question: How the sustainability assessment and evaluation frameworks in the district heating and PT evaluation studies are linked, and which method was most used, plus how do they relate to CO2 emissions reduction in the urban transport example?

The district heating (DH) study and the PT (public transport) evaluation studies are linked only at a methodological level: both use sustainability assessment frameworks based on multi-criteria decision analysis (MCDA) to compare alternatives against multiple economic, environmental, and social criteria. In the DH paper, the comparison is explicitly among WSM, TOPSIS, PROMETHEE, ELECTRE, and DEA, with sensitivity analysis of criterion weights and a comparison of AHP-derived versus equal weights. In the PT study, a hybrid MCDA framework combines fuzzy best-worst method (FBWM) for criterion weighting and MABAC for ranking alternatives, with criteria drawn from literature and experts. (daugavietis2022acomparisonof chunk 1, keshavarzghorabaee2021sustainablepublictransportation chunk 1)

The most used method in the DH sustainability literature cited in the excerpt is not stated as a single dominant method beyond the set WSM, TOPSIS, PROMETHEE, ELECTRE, and DEA; however, the excerpt indicates these are the methods frequently applied in district heating sustainability studies. (daugavietis2022acomparisonof chunk 1)

By contrast, the urban transport carbon-emissions example is not an MCDA ranking study but an LCA/GWP-based scenario analysis. It links sustainability assessment to CO2 emissions reduction by quantifying passenger-transport greenhouse-gas impacts across eight mobility scenarios, showing reductions up to 64.28% when trips and travel distances are reduced. Thus, it complements the MCDA-based DH and PT studies by evaluating sustainability directly through life-cycle carbon mitigation rather than through weighted multi-criteria ranking. (montoyatorres2023towardssustainablepassenger chunk 1)
